name: Constantine the Great
info: Constantine I, known as Constantine the Great (272–337), was Roman emperor from 306 and sole ruler from 324, the first emperor to convert to Christianity, who legalised the faith and founded Constantinople as the empire's capital.

facts.born: 27 February 272 (the year is not recorded; scholars have proposed 271 to 280) at Naissus in Moesia Superior, now Niš in Serbia; son of the army officer Flavius Constantius, later one of the four emperors of the Tetrarchy, and of Helena, a Greek woman of low social standing
facts.died: 22 May 337 at the suburban villa of Achyron near Nicomedia, of an illness that began after Easter, having been baptised on his deathbed by Eusebius of Nicomedia
facts.role: Roman emperor (augustus) from 306, acclaimed by his army at Eboracum and recognised by Galerius as caesar; ruler of the West after 312; sole emperor from 324 to 337
facts.known: the victory at the Milvian Bridge in 312; the Edict of Milan of 313, agreed with Licinius; the founding of Constantinople, dedicated in 330; convoking the First Council of Nicaea in 325; the gold solidus; the execution of his son Crispus and his wife Fausta in 326

t: Proclaimed emperor by his father's army at York in 306, Constantine won the civil wars of the Tetrarchy against Maxentius and Licinius and ruled the whole empire from 324.

He ended the persecution of Christians, legalised their religion with Licinius in 313, convoked the Council of Nicaea and built churches such as the Holy Sepulchre, though scholars still debate the depth of his own faith.

His new capital, Constantinople, and his gold solidus outlasted him by centuries, while his dynastic succession replaced Diocletian's Tetrarchy and his reputation has swung between saint and ruthless politician.
dyk: The gold solidus Constantine introduced, 72 of which made a pound of gold, was struck at a similar weight and purity for seven centuries.
ev: Born at Naissus in Moesia Superior, the son of Flavius Constantius and Helena
On his father's death at Eboracum (York), proclaimed augustus by the army
Defeats Maxentius at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge and enters Rome
Agrees with Licinius at Milan on the edict granting tolerance to Christianity and all religions
Defeats Licinius at Chrysopolis, becomes sole emperor and founds Constantinople
Convokes the First Council of Nicaea, which produces the Nicene Creed
Has his eldest son Crispus put to death and his wife Fausta killed
Baptised on his deathbed by Eusebius of Nicomedia, dies near Nicomedia and is buried in Constantinople

sections.early:
Constantine was born on 27 February 272 at Naissus in Moesia Superior, now Niš in Serbia; his birthday is recorded, but not the year, which scholars have placed between 271 and 280. His father, Flavius Constantius, was an officer in Emperor Aurelian's bodyguard who rose to be governor of Dalmatia. His mother, Helena, was a Greek woman of low social standing, possibly from Drepanum in Bithynia, and it is uncertain whether she was Constantius's wife or his concubine. Around 288 or 289 Constantius left her to marry Theodora, the stepdaughter of the emperor Maximian, and in 293 he was made a caesar in Diocletian's new Tetrarchy.

Constantine was sent to Diocletian's court at Nicomedia as his father's heir presumptive and, since the tetrarchs did not trust one another, as something of a hostage. There he learned Latin literature, Greek and philosophy, and may have heard the Christian scholar Lactantius; his own language was Latin, and he later needed translators at church councils held in Greek. He campaigned on the Danube in 296, against the Persians in Syria in 297 and in Mesopotamia in 298–299. He was in Nicomedia in 303 when Diocletian began the Great Persecution, the most severe persecution of Christians in Roman history. He probably played no part in it, and nothing shows that he opposed it effectively at the time.
sections.rise:
When Diocletian and Maximian abdicated on 1 May 305, Constantine and Maximian's son Maxentius were passed over. Ancient sources tell of plots by Galerius against his life, though how far these tales can be trusted is uncertain. Constantine left the court to join his father, campaigned with him against the Picts, and when Constantius died at Eboracum (York) on 25 July 306 the army proclaimed him augustus. Galerius, furious, granted him only the rank of caesar. Ruling Britain, Gaul and Spain from Trier, he threw back a Frankish invasion and had the captured kings Ascaric and Merogais and their soldiers fed to the beasts in the city's amphitheatre.

In 307 he married Maximian's daughter Fausta. When Maximian rebelled against him in 310, Constantine captured him at Massilia and encouraged his suicide; Maximian hanged himself in July 310, and his memory was condemned. A claimed descent from Claudius II and a vision of Apollo, proclaimed in a speech of 310 and very probably fictions, gave Constantine a new title to rule. In the spring of 312 he crossed the Alps with about 40,000 men, won at Turin and Verona, and on 28 October met Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge. Lactantius says a dream told him to mark his soldiers' shields with the sign of Christ; Eusebius describes a cross of light in the sky. Maxentius drowned in the Tiber, and his head was paraded through Rome.
sections.deeds:
In Rome Constantine disbanded the Praetorian Guard and promised the Senate a secure role. In 313 he and Licinius agreed at Milan on the edict granting full tolerance to Christianity and all religions and returning property seized in the persecution. The two emperors fell out and fought at Cibalae in 314 or 316 and at Mardia in 317; in 324 Constantine won at Adrianople, the Hellespont and Chrysopolis and became sole emperor. That year he founded his new capital at Byzantium, dedicated on 11 May 330 as Constantinople.

He gave the Church money and privileges, promoted Christians to high office and built basilicas, among them the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and Old St Peter's. In 321 he made Sunday a day of rest, and in 325 he summoned the First Council of Nicaea, which dealt with Arianism and produced the Nicene Creed. His reign set a precedent for emperors' authority over church councils. He also reformed the state: civil and military authorities were separated, the army was divided into mobile comitatenses and frontier limitanei, many offices were raised to senatorial rank in 326, and the gold solidus, 72 to the pound, became the standard coin. Between 331 and 336 the gold, silver and bronze statues of pagan temples were declared imperial property and melted down for coinage.
sections.opponents:
Constantine could be ruthless with his rivals and his own family. Licinius and Martinian surrendered on his promise to spare them, but in 325 he accused Licinius of plotting and had both hanged; Licinius's son was killed in 326. In 326 his eldest son Crispus was put to death by "cold poison" at Pola, and in July his wife Fausta was killed in an overheated bath. Few ancient sources discuss why, and those that do are late and generally unreliable; Adrian Goldsworthy speculates that Constantine wished to keep a firm grip on his heirs. He also used force against Christians he judged schismatic, ordering in 317 that the property of the Donatists in North Africa be confiscated and their clergy exiled, and some of his laws on the Jews were unfavourable, though not harsher than his predecessors'. His panegyrist declared that "It is a stupid clemency that spares the conquered foe."

His critics began in his own family. His nephew Julian the Apostate called him inferior to the great pagan emperors and given over to luxury and greed, and Eunapius and Zosimus blamed him for weakening the empire through indulgence to the Christians. The author of De rebus bellicis held that his monetary policy widened the gap between rich and poor. Edward Gibbon described him as a war hero "degenerating into a cruel and dissolute monarch" in old age, and Jacob Burckhardt saw a scheming secularist who manipulated every party to secure his power.
sections.last:
Constantine lived much of his later life in Constantinople. In 328 a bridge over the Danube at Sucidava was completed in the hope of reconquering Dacia; he campaigned with the Sarmatians against the Goths in 332 and against the Sarmatians themselves in 334, settling some of their exiles as farmers and conscripting the rest, and he took the title Dacicus maximus in 336. When Prince Narseh invaded Armenia in 336 and set a Persian client on its throne, Constantine prepared a war he treated as a Christian crusade, with bishops to accompany the army and a tent in the shape of a church. He turned away Persian envoys seeking peace, but the campaign was called off when he fell ill in the spring of 337.

After Easter he went to the baths near Helenopolis, then to the suburbs of Nicomedia, where he asked for baptism, which he had long put off; the Arian bishop Eusebius of Nicomedia baptised him. He died at the villa of Achyron on 22 May 337. Eusebius places his death after the Persian campaign, while most other sources put it in the middle of the preparations, and some scholars conclude that the Vita was edited to defend his reputation. He was buried in a porphyry sarcophagus in the Church of the Holy Apostles. His three sons by Fausta, Constantine II, Constantius II and Constans, succeeded him, and followers of Constantius killed several relatives, among them the nephews Dalmatius and Hannibalianus.
sections.legacy:
Constantine replaced Diocletian's Tetrarchy with dynastic succession, and the age of Constantine marked a turn from classical antiquity towards the Middle Ages. Constantinople remained the capital of the empire for more than a thousand years, and the solidus was struck at a similar weight and purity for seven centuries. In Byzantium it became a great honour to be hailed as a "new Constantine", and ten emperors bore his name; Charlemagne, Henry VIII, Philip II of Spain and several dynasties claimed descent from him. The Eastern Orthodox and Eastern Catholic Churches venerate him as isapostolos, equal of the Apostles, with his mother Helena on 21 May. The Donation of Constantine, an 8th-century document in which he grants Rome and the West to Pope Sylvester, was long accepted as the basis of papal temporal power until Lorenzo Valla proved it a forgery in 1440.

The sources are abundant but shaped by official propaganda. Eusebius's Vita Constantini, written between 335 and 339, mixes eulogy and hagiography, and modern historians have often challenged its reliability. The medieval church held Constantine up as a paragon, while the rediscovery of hostile sources in the Renaissance brought more critical views. Modern scholars still disagree about his faith: Henri Grégoire thought he took up Christianity for its political use, Timothy Barnes saw a radical convert on a personal crusade, and Peter Heather argues that he was raised a Christian and revealed it in stages.

summary: Constantine rose from his father's army in Britain to win the civil wars of the Tetrarchy and rule the whole Roman Empire from 324. He legalised Christianity, convoked the Council of Nicaea and founded Constantinople, and he also killed his rivals, his son and his wife; ancient propaganda and modern scholarship have left his faith and his motives disputed.
